t: #2617 Minimum Number of Visited Cells in a Grid
o: Plain BFS is O(mn·maxJump) which blows up on 1e5 cells with jumps up to 1e5. The fix: never re-scan cells. For each row keep a 'next unvisited column' pointer structure, and similarly for each column; when expanding a cell, repeatedly jump to the next unvisited reachable cell via these structures. Union-Find with path compression gives near-O(1) 'next free slot' queries, making total work nearly linear. Once (m-1, n-1) is reached, return its distance.
k: BFS guarantees minimum visits; the challenge is enumerating reachable neighbors cheaply.
Union-Find 'next unvisited index' per row and per column skips visited cells in amortized near-O(1).
Each cell is claimed at most once across all expansions, so total work is near-linear.

a.i: Maintain DSU arrays nxtRow[i][c] and nxtCol[j][r] pointing to the next unvisited cell; after visiting a cell, union it forward so future finds skip it.
s: Initialize DSU parents: for row i, parent[c] = c for c in 0..n (sentinel n); likewise columns.
BFS from (0,0) with distances; pop cell (i,j) with jump g = grid[i][j].
Right moves: repeatedly find next free column > j in row i while <= j+g and < n; claim each, push with dist+1, union it to the next. Same for down moves in column j.
If the goal is popped, return its distance; if the queue empties, return -1.

c.python:
from collections import deque
class Solution:
    def minimumVisitedCells(self, grid: list[list[int]]) -> int:
        m, n = len(grid), len(grid[0])
        rowP = [list(range(n + 1)) for _ in range(m)]
        colP = [list(range(m + 1)) for _ in range(n)]
        def find(p, x):
            while p[x] != x:
                p[x] = p[p[x]]
                x = p[x]
            return x
        dist = [[-1] * n for _ in range(m)]
        dist[0][0] = 1
        dq = deque([(0, 0)])
        while dq:
            i, j = dq.popleft()
            if i == m - 1 and j == n - 1: return dist[i][j]
            g = grid[i][j]
            x = find(rowP[i], j + 1)
            while x <= min(j + g, n - 1):
                dist[i][x] = dist[i][j] + 1
                dq.append((i, x))
                rowP[i][x] = x + 1
                x = find(rowP[i], x + 1)
            y = find(colP[j], i + 1)
            while y <= min(i + g, m - 1):
                if dist[y][j] == -1:
                    dist[y][j] = dist[i][j] + 1
                    dq.append((y, j))
                colP[j][y] = y + 1
                y = find(colP[j], y + 1)
        return -1

a.t: O(mn · α(mn)) — each cell is claimed once and DSU finds are amortized near-constant
a.sp: O(mn) for the DSU structures and distance grid

a.n: Approach 2: BFS + Sorted Sets per Row/Column
a.i: Same idea but with balanced BSTs (sorted containers) holding unvisited indices per row/column; erase visited cells as you go.
s: Keep a sorted set of unvisited columns for each row and rows for each column.
When expanding, use range queries to fetch and erase all unvisited cells within jump range.
BFS as usual; answer when the goal is dequeued.

c.python:
from collections import deque
from sortedcontainers import SortedList
class Solution:
    def minimumVisitedCells(self, grid: list[list[int]]) -> int:
        m, n = len(grid), len(grid[0])
        rows = [SortedList(range(n)) for _ in range(m)]
        cols = [SortedList(range(m)) for _ in range(n)]
        dist = [[-1] * n for _ in range(m)]
        dist[0][0] = 1
        dq = deque([(0, 0)])
        while dq:
            i, j = dq.popleft()
            if i == m - 1 and j == n - 1: return dist[i][j]
            g = grid[i][j]
            for x in list(rows[i].irange(j + 1, min(j + g, n - 1))):
                rows[i].remove(x); cols[x].remove(i)
                dist[i][x] = dist[i][j] + 1
                dq.append((i, x))
            for y in list(cols[j].irange(i + 1, min(i + g, m - 1))):
                cols[j].remove(y); rows[y].remove(j)
                dist[y][j] = dist[i][j] + 1
                dq.append((y, j))
        return -1

a.t: O(mn log(mn)) — each cell inserted/erased once from two ordered structures
a.sp: O(mn) for the sets and distance grid

w: Approach 1 (DSU) is faster and allocation-friendly; Approach 2 is easier to reason about if a sorted-container library exists. Pitfall: the start cell counts as visited (answer includes it), and grid[m-1][n-1]=0 means the goal has no outgoing moves. Watch duplicate pushes in the column loop — guard with a distance check. Follow-up: weighted jumps would require Dijkstra with the same skipping trick.
